note_tweet.text:
Condensates, semiliquid droplets of concentrated proteins, are a “hot area in biology,” says biologist Chris Holland. 

They help mold squid beaks and allow mussels to adhere themselves to rocks. And recently, new research reveals that they also help give spider silk its characteristic strength. 

Each of these strong yet flexible materials are tougher than much of what humans can build synthetically. Scientists dream of making spider silk into high-performing materials for seat belts, helmets, naval materials, and even scaffolds to help repair brain cells. But attempts to make the material in the lab have fallen short. Kevlar, a synthetic fiber, is currently our toughest material, but it requires processing at very high temperatures and acidic conditions.

“Here, you have an organism like a spider or a mussel, which is basically making a superior material under ambient conditions in seawater or in just plain air,” said biological materials scientist Matthew Harrington. 

🕸️ Learn more on our web-site: https://t.co/T4VGrHJEsp

note_tweet.text:
UK PM SAYS OPEN TO SLAVERY APOLOGY, BUT RULES OUT REPARATIONS

British PM #AndyBurnham says he is open to a formal apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic #slavetrade, but has ruled out financial reparations.

Ahead of next week's Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, Burnham acknowledged #slavery's lasting legacy but argued that today's British taxpayers should not foot the bill for crimes committed centuries ago.

Instead, he proposed a debt initiative to help poorer Commonwealth nations secure longer repayment periods and lower interest rates.

British ships forcibly transported more than 3 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic before Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807. 

Hundreds of thousands died during the crossing. Britain has never formally apologized for its role in slavery.
